Lindsay Clancy's defense is asking Judge Sullivan to enter a finding of not guilty after her first trial ended in a mistrial. One of Kevin Reddington's arguments is that prosecutors never presented sufficient evidence proving Clancy committed the underlying acts. The prosecution's response was direct: after hearing the defense repeatedly say during trial that Clancy had admitted or stipulated to the underlying conduct, the prosecutor called the new sufficiency argument “laughable” and began laying out the evidence supporting the murder charges.

dy5ro2L7hkM.title: Lindsay Clancy Wants A NOT GUILTY Verdict Without A New Trial
dy5ro2L7hkM.description:
Lindsay Clancy's first trial ended without a verdict. Now her defense is asking Judge Sullivan to enter a finding of not guilty himself. Kevin Reddington argues that prosecutors failed to present sufficient evidence to prove the underlying charges beyond a reasonable doubt—and separately argues that the state failed to overcome Clancy's lack-of-criminal-responsibility defense. It's an attempt to end the case without waiting for another jury.  

I walk through Reddington's argument and explain the enormous problem I see with it. The first trial was fought primarily over Lindsay Clancy's mental state, with the defense relying on lack of criminal responsibility. Now Reddington is attacking whether the state sufficiently proved the underlying conduct in the first place. I explain why that creates a major tension with how the defense tried the case, what the legal standard actually requires, and whether Judge Sullivan could really enter a not-guilty finding after the mistrial.

j4qCWU_clDE.title: Does Lindsay Clancy’s Lawyer WANT A New Judge?
j4qCWU_clDE.description:
I'm watching a potentially important timing fight develop in the Lindsay Clancy retrial. Judge William Sullivan made clear that he wants the case moving and specifically referenced getting it tried before his retirement. But when the court pushed for a trial date, Kevin Reddington said he cannot do the trial before June. That's significant because Sullivan reaches Massachusetts' mandatory judicial retirement age in June.   

I break down why I don't think that timing should be ignored. If Sullivan retires before the retrial can be completed, another judge could end up handling the case—and that could reopen important questions involving evidence, witnesses, and other trial rulings. I'll also show you the courtroom exchange that led me to ask whether Reddington would actually prefer another judge. That's my interpretation of the strategy, not something Reddington expressly admitted.

Eddie Duran took the stand and described the moments before he shot Air Force Senior Airman Roger Fortson. Duran also explained why he approached the apartment alone, why he initially knocked without announcing himself, and why he fired five times.

What matters is whether Duran reasonably perceived an imminent threat of unlawful deadly force. I'll explain why that distinction is critical, what Duran's testimony establishes about his claimed perception, and why the prosecution's upcoming cross-examination could be decisive.
